plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates how the 3D motion of a point projects into 2D motion on the image plane under a pinhole camera model. A 3D point P moves through space with instantaneous velocity Ṗ, and the green line from the camera center O through P shows the projection ray, which pierces the image plane at the corresponding 2D image point p. The red arrow at P labeled Ṗ marks the point's 3D velocity, while the red arrow at p labeled ṗ marks the resulting instantaneous velocity of its 2D projection; the dashed line traces where the displaced 3D point projects, making clear that the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity rather than a simple rescaling of it. This figure motivates the perspective-projection relations x = fX/Z and y = fY/Z, and their time derivatives, as the mathematical link between a point's 3D velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) in world coordinates and its observed 2D optical flow ṗ = (ẋ, ẏ) in the camera plane.

elements: camera center O — black sphere at the origin, label 'o' below-left of it
image plane — vertical semi-transparent rectangle perpendicular to the optical axis at z = f, with a dark grey border frame
3D point P — black sphere far to the right of the plane, label 'P' to its right
image point p — smaller black sphere sitting exactly on the image plane where the ray pierces it, label 'p' below-right
solid bright-green projection ray from O through p to P, extended slightly past P
red 3D velocity arrow Ṗ anchored at P, pointing up and back toward the camera, label 'Ṗ' above it
dashed bright-green ray from O to the displaced point P+Ṗ, piercing the plane at the displaced image point
red 2D velocity arrow ṗ anchored at p, lying in the image plane, pointing up-left, label 'ṗ' above-left

interactions.teaches: Dragging P anywhere in 3D makes p slide across the image plane along the ray from O — the image point is always the intersection of the viewing ray with the plane, so the same 3D displacement produces less image motion when P is farther away

interactions.label: Ẋ — lateral velocity
interactions.teaches: Lateral 3D velocity produces roughly horizontal optical flow whose magnitude is scaled by f/Z — the same speed looks smaller in the image for a more distant point

interactions.label: Ẏ — vertical velocity
interactions.teaches: Vertical 3D velocity produces vertical optical flow, again attenuated by depth through the f/Z factor

interactions.label: Ż — depth velocity
interactions.teaches: Motion along the viewing direction produces no image motion on-axis and expansion/contraction flow off-axis (looming) — a purely projective effect with no orthographic counterpart
Rotating the scene reveals the true 3D geometry that the single textbook viewpoint flattens: p lies exactly where the segment OP pierces the image plane, and ṗ is that piercing point's motion

demo_steps.title: As drawn in the book
demo_steps.narration: The figure's configuration: Ṗ has vertical and toward-camera components. The dashed ray to the displaced point P+Ṗ pierces the plane exactly at the tip of the ṗ arrow — the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity.

demo_steps.title: Pure lateral motion
demo_steps.narration: With only Ẋ nonzero, ṗ becomes horizontal with magnitude f·Ẋ/Z — a clean rescaling. This is the component that behaves most intuitively.

demo_steps.title: Pure depth motion
demo_steps.narration: With only Ż nonzero (moving toward the camera), p drifts outward from the principal point even though P's X and Y never change — perspective division by Z turns approach into looming expansion.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World setup: camera center O at origin; optical axis along +Z into the scene (screen-right in the source); image plane at z = f = 2, a vertical rectangle spanning X∈[−1.5,1.5], Y∈[−2,2] — tall, as in the source. Initial P = (0.8, 0.9, 7); then p = (fX/Z, fY/Z, f) ≈ (0.23, 0.26, 2), sitting ON the plane slightly right of and above its center — in the source p is left of the plane's vertical midline region and the ray from O rises gently to the right toward P. Scene spans x∈[−2,3], y∈[−2,2.5], z∈[0,8]; look-at ≈ (0.4, 0.2, 3.5). Sizes: O sphere r=0.18, P sphere r=0.18, p sphere r=0.11, all black #111111. Solid ray: thick bright green #33dd33 line from O through p to P, extended ~8% past P. Velocity display scale s = 1.2 world units per unit velocity: red arrow #ee1111 from P to P+s·Ṗ; with default Ṗ=(−0.5,1,−1) it points up and back toward O, matching the source. Dashed green ray (same color) from O to P' = P+s·Ṗ. Displaced image point p' = exact reprojection of P' onto z=f; red ṗ arrow from p to p', lying in the plane — its tip must coincide with where the dashed ray pierces the plane (for small s this equals the linearized flow). Formulas needed: p=(fX/Z, fY/Z); ẋ = f(ẊZ − XŻ)/Z², ẏ = f(ẎZ − YŻ)/Z². Labels are serif-italic black text: 'o' below-left of O, 'P' right of P, 'p' below-right of p, 'Ṗ' above the red arrow at P, 'ṗ' above-left of the red arrow at p. Plane fill light grey #cccccc at ~0.2 opacity, border #444444. Background white.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.ArrowHelper for both red velocity arrows and rebuild/re-aim them on every state change. Dashed ray via THREE.LineDashedMaterial — call computeLineDistances() after each geometry update or dashes collapse. Drag: raycast pointer onto a drag plane parallel to the image plane at P's current z, clamp X∈[−2,3], Y∈[−2,2.5], keep Z fixed during a drag; then recompute p, both rays, and both arrows every frame from (P, Ṗ) — never move p independently. Render labels with CSS2DRenderer or canvas sprites in a serif italic face so ṗ/Ṗ read as dotted symbols. Keep the image plane static; only P-driven geometry updates.

authoredContext:
A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$,
in camera coordinates (-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the
point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of
$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The
projection of this point into the image plane location is
$\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D
instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
where all the derivatives are done with respect to time, $t$.

A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.

Demo steps

discrepancies: Composition is mirrored relative to the source: in the book O is at the lower-left and P at the far right, while the generated view places P on the left and O on the right
The image plane is much smaller than in the source, where the plane dominates the left half of the figure as a large tall rectangle; here it is a small grey panel in the middle
The green rays are thin 1px lines, whereas the source shows bold solid and dashed green rays with strong visual weight

The source shows the dashed green ray continuing past the plane to the tip of Ṗ with the ṗ arrow tip exactly at the piercing point; the generated default does show this, but the arrowheads and rays are visually faint compared to the bold red arrows in the book
Labels (o, P, p, Ṗ, ṗ) are present but noticeably small compared to the large serif labels in the source
evaluation.notes: All core elements (O, plane, P, p, solid/dashed rays, Ṗ and ṗ arrows) are present and the projection/velocity math is correct, with excellent sliders, demo steps, and drag interaction; main issues are the mirrored default view, an undersized image plane, and thin/faint rays versus the bold source styling.
action_items: Change the default camera azimuth so O sits at lower-left and P at far right, matching the source composition
Enlarge the image plane (e.g. 4x5 or bigger) so it dominates one side of the frame as in the book
Render the green rays as thick cylinders (or fat lines) to match the bold solid/dashed rays in the source
Increase label font sizes, especially for P, p, Ṗ, and ṗ, to match the large serif hierarchy of the original

feedback.rationale: Concept and interactivity are excellent (5s), but the mirrored camera composition, undersized image plane, thin rays, and small labels are concrete implementation-level fixes the generator can address without any plan changes.

interactions.teaches: Lateral 3D velocity produces roughly horizontal optical flow whose magnitude is scaled by f/Z — the same speed looks smaller in the image for a more distant point

interactions.label: Ẏ — vertical velocity
interactions.teaches: Vertical 3D velocity produces vertical optical flow, again attenuated by depth through the f/Z factor

interactions.label: Ż — depth velocity
interactions.teaches: Motion along the viewing direction produces no image motion on-axis and expansion/contraction flow off-axis (looming) — a purely projective effect with no orthographic counterpart
Rotating the scene reveals the true 3D geometry that the single textbook viewpoint flattens: p lies exactly where the segment OP pierces the image plane, and ṗ is that piercing point's motion

demo_steps.title: As drawn in the book
demo_steps.narration: The figure's configuration: Ṗ has vertical and toward-camera components. The dashed ray to the displaced point P+Ṗ pierces the plane exactly at the tip of the ṗ arrow — the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity.

demo_steps.title: Pure lateral motion
demo_steps.narration: With only Ẋ nonzero, ṗ becomes horizontal with magnitude f·Ẋ/Z — a clean rescaling. This is the component that behaves most intuitively.

demo_steps.title: Pure depth motion
demo_steps.narration: With only Ż nonzero (moving toward the camera), p drifts outward from the principal point even though P's X and Y never change — perspective division by Z turns approach into looming expansion.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World setup: camera center O at origin; optical axis along +Z into the scene (screen-right in the source); image plane at z = f = 2, a vertical rectangle spanning X∈[−1.5,1.5], Y∈[−2,2] — tall, as in the source. Initial P = (0.8, 0.9, 7); then p = (fX/Z, fY/Z, f) ≈ (0.23, 0.26, 2), sitting ON the plane slightly right of and above its center — in the source p is left of the plane's vertical midline region and the ray from O rises gently to the right toward P. Scene spans x∈[−2,3], y∈[−2,2.5], z∈[0,8]; look-at ≈ (0.4, 0.2, 3.5). Sizes: O sphere r=0.18, P sphere r=0.18, p sphere r=0.11, all black #111111. Solid ray: thick bright green #33dd33 line from O through p to P, extended ~8% past P. Velocity display scale s = 1.2 world units per unit velocity: red arrow #ee1111 from P to P+s·Ṗ; with default Ṗ=(−0.5,1,−1) it points up and back toward O, matching the source. Dashed green ray (same color) from O to P' = P+s·Ṗ. Displaced image point p' = exact reprojection of P' onto z=f; red ṗ arrow from p to p', lying in the plane — its tip must coincide with where the dashed ray pierces the plane (for small s this equals the linearized flow). Formulas needed: p=(fX/Z, fY/Z); ẋ = f(ẊZ − XŻ)/Z², ẏ = f(ẎZ − YŻ)/Z². Labels are serif-italic black text: 'o' below-left of O, 'P' right of P, 'p' below-right of p, 'Ṗ' above the red arrow at P, 'ṗ' above-left of the red arrow at p. Plane fill light grey #cccccc at ~0.2 opacity, border #444444. Background white.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.ArrowHelper for both red velocity arrows and rebuild/re-aim them on every state change. Dashed ray via THREE.LineDashedMaterial — call computeLineDistances() after each geometry update or dashes collapse. Drag: raycast pointer onto a drag plane parallel to the image plane at P's current z, clamp X∈[−2,3], Y∈[−2,2.5], keep Z fixed during a drag; then recompute p, both rays, and both arrows every frame from (P, Ṗ) — never move p independently. Render labels with CSS2DRenderer or canvas sprites in a serif italic face so ṗ/Ṗ read as dotted symbols. Keep the image plane static; only P-driven geometry updates.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates how the 3D motion of a point projects into 2D motion on the image plane under a pinhole camera model. A 3D point P moves through space with instantaneous velocity Ṗ, and the green line from the camera center O through P shows the projection ray, which pierces the image plane at the corresponding 2D image point p. The red arrow at P labeled Ṗ marks the point's 3D velocity, while the red arrow at p labeled ṗ marks the resulting instantaneous velocity of its 2D projection; the dashed line traces where the displaced 3D point projects, making clear that the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity rather than a simple rescaling of it. This figure motivates the perspective-projection relations x = fX/Z and y = fY/Z, and their time derivatives, as the mathematical link between a point's 3D velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) in world coordinates and its observed 2D optical flow ṗ = (ẋ, ẏ) in the camera plane.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag the 3D point P along its trajectory and watch the 2D projection p move on the image plane
- Sliders for velocity components (X-dot, Y-dot, Z-dot) to show how each affects the 2D optical flow vector

discrepancies: Composition is horizontally mirrored: in the source, O is at the left and P at the far right, but the generated view shows P on the left and o on the right, reversing the depth arrangement of the figure
The image plane in the source is a large panel dominating the left half of the figure; in the generated figure it is a modestly sized rectangle in the middle
The solid green ray in the source terminates at P, while the generated version extends 8% past P
The source ṗ arrow points along the plane away from p in a clear horizontal direction; the generated ṗ arrow is short and partially obscured by the p sphere at default settings
evaluation.notes: All primitives, labels, and the projected-velocity concept are correct, and the sliders plus demo steps are pedagogically excellent, but the default camera mirrors the source's left-right depth composition (P and O swapped sides) and the image plane is much less dominant than in the original.
action_items: Adjust the camera azimuth/orbit orientation so the default view matches the source: O at the left, image plane in the middle-left, and P at the right
Enlarge the image plane (and/or reposition it) so it dominates the left half of the composition as in the source
End the solid green ray at P instead of overshooting by a factor of 1.08

feedback.rationale: Concept accuracy and interactivity are perfect (5s) with a correct plan, but the default camera mirrors the composition, the image plane is undersized, and the ray overshoots P — all concrete implementation fixes for the generator.
